parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Thornbury (TB)**
> 
> Thornbury (TB) supplies gas and electricity to homes in country W. It employs 4,000 people across a head office, three regional centres and a field engineering team.
> 
> TB's HR department keeps personnel records on paper at each location. Holiday requests, training records and absence data are held separately and are not shared between sites.
> 
> **Table 1.1: TB selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 4,000 |
> |---|---|
> | HR staff | 34 |
> | Average time to answer an employee query about pay or holiday (working days) | 6 |
> | Employees whose training records could not be located last year | 310 |
> | Cost of a proposed integrated HR system (\$000) | 1,400 |
> | Estimated annual saving in HR staff time (\$000) | 290 |
> 
> TB's finance director notes that the system would take almost five years to repay its cost.

Evaluate whether TB should invest in an integrated HR system.
parts.solution_md:
An integrated system would hold every employee record in one place **[K]**. TB currently keeps paper records separately at a head office, three regional centres and among a field team, and last year it could not locate the training records of 310 employees **[Ap]**. Missing training records matter enormously in an energy business, because TB may be unable to prove that an engineer working on gas equipment holds the qualifications the law requires, which exposes it to both danger and prosecution **[An]**

However, the system costs \$1.4m against an estimated saving of \$290,000 a year **[K]**. On those figures TB waits almost five years before the investment repays itself, and that assumes the saving is achieved in full **[Ap]**. Large system projects frequently overrun, and 34 HR staff across four locations would need training and time to change how they work, during which the saving would be smaller than forecast **[An]**

The payback period looks unattractive, but it measures only the saving TB has been able to quantify **[E]**. The 310 missing training records represent a compliance risk whose cost is not \$290,000 a year but whatever a single serious incident or prosecution would cost, which could exceed the entire \$1.4m **[E]**. A six-day wait for an answer about pay is also a real if unmeasured cost, since 4,000 employees are being poorly served by their own employer **[E]**. The finance director is right to question a five-year payback on cash grounds alone, but the decision should not rest on cash grounds alone **[E]**. TB should invest, though it would be prudent to introduce the system in one regional centre first, so that problems surface before all 4,000 records depend on it **[E]**

>

>

Records split across four locations and never shared mean TB cannot see its own workforce as a whole, and 310 untraceable training records is not an administrative irritation but a failure to evidence competence in an industry where engineers work on gas. However, the system costs \$1.4m against an estimated saving of \$290,000 a year, so it takes almost five years to repay on the figures TB has quantified
> - A single system would let TB plan across the whole workforce, identifying skills shortages and upcoming retirements that separate paper files at four sites make effectively invisible. However, large system projects commonly cost more and take longer than planned, and 34 HR staff across four locations would have to run old and new processes in parallel while they learn
> - A six-working-day wait for an answer about pay or holiday tells 4,000 employees that their employer is disorganised, which affects morale and consumes management time in chasing. However, this cost is real but unmeasured, so it cannot be set against the \$1.4m in the way the finance director's payback calculation can
> - The quantified saving captures only HR staff time, whereas the compliance exposure from missing training records could exceed the whole \$1.4m if a single serious incident or prosecution followed. However, that exposure is a risk rather than a certainty, and TB has no way of knowing how likely it is
> - TB could introduce the system in one regional centre first, testing it and refining the estimate before committing the full amount. However, phasing delays the benefit and means TB runs two systems side by side for longer, which would reduce the saving in the meantime
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Kingsmere (KM)**
> 
> Kingsmere (KM) is an estate agency with 31 branches in country B, employing 280 negotiators who value homes and sell them.
> 
> Negotiators are currently judged only on the number of properties they sell each month, and a monthly bonus is paid to the top ten performers.
> 
> **Table 1.1: KM selected data**
> 
> | Branches | 31 |
> |---|---|
> | Negotiators | 280 |
> | Average properties sold per negotiator per month | 3.4 |
> | Properties valued above the eventual selling price (%) | 44 |
> | Sales that fell through before completion (%) | 27 |
> | Customer satisfaction score (out of 10) | 6.4 |
> 
> KM's HR director proposes judging negotiators on a combination of sales completed, valuation accuracy and customer satisfaction.

Evaluate whether KM should change how it measures the performance of its negotiators.
parts.solution_md:
A single measure encourages employees to maximise that measure whatever else happens **[K]**. KM judges negotiators only on properties sold, and 44% of properties are valued above what they eventually sell for, while 27% of sales collapse before completion **[Ap]**. Over-valuing a house wins the instruction from the seller, which counts towards the sales figure, but it also makes the sale far harder to complete, so the present measure is rewarding behaviour that damages KM **[An]**

However, a combined measure is harder to operate **[K]**. Sales completed can be counted exactly, whereas valuation accuracy and a satisfaction score of 6.4 out of 10 depend on judgement and on customers choosing to respond **[Ap]**. Negotiators may distrust a bonus resting partly on measures they feel they cannot control, and a measure staff do not accept as fair tends to demotivate rather than direct **[An]**

KM should change the measure, because the present one is actively causing the problem it needs to solve **[E]**. A negotiator behaving exactly as KM rewards them to behave produces inflated valuations and collapsed sales, so the fault lies in the measure rather than in the staff **[E]**. The concern about fairness is real, but it argues for designing the new measure carefully rather than for keeping a broken one **[E]**. Weighting completed sales most heavily, with valuation accuracy and satisfaction as smaller components, would keep the measure understandable while removing the incentive to over-value **[E]**. KM should also expect the change to take time, since negotiators who have built their habits around a single target will not adjust the week the rules change **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> - A full-mark answer will include

> - Detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning
> - Evaluation of relevant issues which leads to a conclusion supported by strong reasoning
> - The importance of at least two points must be identified and analysed
> 
> **Knowledge and application**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |

> | **4** | - Shows understanding of two ways of measuring employee performance in context |
> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one way of measuring employee performance in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two ways of measuring employee performance |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one way of measuring employee performance |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two ways of measuring employee performance in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one way of measuring employee performance in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two ways of measuring employee performance |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one way of measuring employee performance |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - KM could adopt the HR director's combined measure of sales completed, valuation accuracy and customer satisfaction. Counting only properties sold rewards winning instructions rather than completing sales, which is why 44% of valuations exceed the eventual price and 27% of sales collapse, so a broader measure removes the incentive to over-value. However, satisfaction depends on who chooses to respond and valuation accuracy is only known with hindsight, so negotiators may see the new measure as resting on things they cannot control
> - KM could keep the existing single measure. Sales completed is objective, undisputed and easily understood, and a bonus staff regard as fair motivates more reliably than one they distrust. However, the present measure is producing exactly the behaviour it pays for, and that behaviour is costing KM completions, so keeping it means keeping the cause of the problem
> - Including satisfaction would give KM a route to lift a score of 6.4 out of 10, which matters in a market where sellers choose an agent largely on reputation and word of mouth. However, satisfaction is influenced by events outside a negotiator's control, such as a buyer withdrawing, so it rewards circumstance as well as performance
> - A 27% fall-through rate wastes negotiator time on sales that never complete, so KM pays for the same work twice and disappoints sellers whose recommendations it needs. However, some fall-through is normal in property and no measure will remove it entirely, so KM must be careful what level it sets as a target
> - Rewarding only the top ten of 280 negotiators means most staff have little realistic prospect of a bonus, so the incentive structure may need attention as much as the measure does. However, widening the bonus raises costs, and KM would need confidence that the resulting change in behaviour justified them
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Vinehall (VH)**
> 
> Vinehall (VH) provides catering for weddings, conferences and corporate events in country R. Demand is highly seasonal, with around 60% of its work falling between May and September.
> 
> VH employs 90 permanent staff and takes on up to 400 casual workers during the busy season. Casual staff are recruited afresh each year, given a two-hour briefing, and paid by the shift.
> 
> **Table 1.1: VH selected data**
> 
> | Permanent staff | 90 |
> |---|---|
> | Casual staff at peak | 400 |
> | Share of annual revenue earned May to September (%) | 60 |
> | Casual staff returning from the previous season (%) | 18 |
> | Events receiving a complaint about service (%) | 14 |
> | Cost of proposed training and guaranteed return contracts (\$000 per year) | 620 |
> 
> VH's operations director argues that better-trained returning staff would reduce complaints. VH's finance director argues that casual labour must stay cheap and flexible because demand collapses in winter.

Evaluate whether VH should adopt a softer approach to human resource management.
parts.solution_md:
Soft HRM treats employees as an asset to be developed rather than a cost to be minimised **[K]**. Only 18% of VH's casual staff return from the previous season, so almost every one of the 400 peak workers is new each year and receives just a two-hour briefing **[Ap]**. Guaranteed return contracts and proper training would build a pool of staff who already know how VH runs an event, which should reduce the 14% of events attracting a complaint about service **[An]**

However, VH's demand is genuinely seasonal **[K]**. Sixty per cent of revenue is earned between May and September, so VH has little work for 400 people during the winter **[Ap]**. Committing \$620,000 a year to training and guaranteed contracts creates a fixed cost in a business whose income is anything but fixed, and in a poor season that commitment would have to be met from much reduced revenue **[An]**

Whether VH should soften its approach depends on how much the complaints are actually costing it **[E]**. Corporate and wedding customers choose caterers largely on reputation, so 14% of events producing a complaint is very likely losing VH future bookings, and that loss may well exceed \$620,000 even though it never appears as a line in the accounts **[E]**. The finance director is right that VH cannot carry 400 people through the winter, but a softer approach need not mean employing everyone permanently **[E]**. VH could offer guaranteed return contracts to a core of perhaps 100 experienced casuals while keeping the rest flexible, lifting the return rate well above 18% at a fraction of the full cost **[E]**. On balance VH should move some way towards soft HRM, but selectively rather than across the whole casual workforce **[E]**

> **Indicative content**
> 
> - VH could adopt soft HRM across its casual workforce, offering training and guaranteed return contracts. An 18% return rate means VH rebuilds almost its entire peak workforce every year, and a two-hour briefing cannot equip 400 people to serve a wedding to the standard clients expect, so complaints at 14% of events are the predictable result. However, committing \$620,000 a year converts a variable cost into a fixed one in a business earning 60% of its revenue in five months
> - VH could keep its current hard approach, treating casual labour as a cost to be minimised and kept flexible. With so little work in winter VH genuinely cannot carry 400 people year-round, and the \$620,000 is certain while the reduction in complaints is not. However, reputation is what wins catering contracts, since customers booking a wedding or conference cannot sample the service first, so the saving may cost more than it protects
> - VH could offer guaranteed return contracts to a core of experienced casuals while keeping the remainder flexible, lifting the return rate well above 18% at a fraction of the full cost. However, this creates two tiers of casual staff, which may cause resentment among those excluded and complicate scheduling at peak
> - The unmeasured cost of lost repeat business and recommendations may well exceed \$620,000 in a market where bookings come largely by word of mouth. However, VH cannot know this precisely, so the decision rests partly on how much weight the directors give to a reputation they cannot put a figure on
> - VH could delay the commitment until forward bookings for the coming season are visible, reducing the risk of fixing costs against income that may not arrive. However, training has to happen before the season starts, so delaying the decision may mean losing the benefit for another year
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Amberley (AM)**
> 
> Amberley (AM) is a retail bank in country K employing 6,800 people across 240 branches and two head offices.
> 
> AM receives around 19,000 applications a year for its graduate training scheme, from which it recruits 120 trainees. Applications are currently read by a team of eight HR staff.
> 
> AM is considering using an AI system to screen applications and rank candidates before any are read by a person.
> 
> **Table 1.1: AM selected data**
> 
> | Graduate applications per year | 19,000 |
> |---|---|
> | Trainees recruited per year | 120 |
> | HR staff currently screening applications | 8 |
> | Average time from application to first interview (weeks) | 11 |
> | Cost of the AI screening system (\$000 per year) | 210 |
> | Applications the AI system would pass to a person (%) | 15 |

Analyse **two** effects on AM of using an AI system to screen job applications.
parts.solution_md:
One effect is that AM would reach candidates far more quickly **[K]**. Eight HR staff currently read all 19,000 applications, which is why it takes eleven weeks from application to first interview **[Ap]**. A system passing only 15% of applications to a person leaves around 2,850 to be read rather than 19,000, so AM could invite candidates to interview in a fraction of the present time **[An]**. That matters because graduates apply to several employers at once, and the strongest are likely to have accepted an offer elsewhere long before AM's eleventh week arrives **[An]** A second effect is that AM would be relying on the system's judgement about who is worth reading at all **[K]**. The AI would reject roughly 16,150 applications a year without any person seeing them **[Ap]**. If it has been trained on AM's own past recruitment decisions, it will tend to favour the same kinds of candidate the bank has always hired, so applicants from different backgrounds or with unusual routes into banking could be filtered out consistently **[An]**. AM would find this very hard to notice, precisely because the rejected applications are never read, so a narrowing of its intake could continue unchallenged for years **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

- The answer makes a basic attempt to explain the causes, impacts or consequences of **one** point | | | | > > **Indicative content** > > - Reducing the reading task from 19,000 applications to around 2,850 removes the bottleneck causing an eleven-week wait; in graduate recruitment speed is competitive, since candidates hold several applications at once and accept the first credible offer > - Applying identical criteria to every application also makes screening more consistent than eight different readers working through 19,000 forms, where fatigue and individual preference inevitably affect who progresses > - The system rejects around 16,150 applications unseen, and if trained on AM's previous hiring it will reproduce whatever patterns those decisions contained; the danger is not simply bias but invisible bias, since nobody reviews what was discarded > - At \$210,000 a year the system is a recurring cost, and AM would need to decide what its eight HR staff now do; if they move to interviewing and candidate contact the spend may be justified, but if the eleven-week delay persists further down the process the saving is lost > > Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Bellfield (BF)**
> 
> Bellfield (BF) owns 62 clothing shops in country S and employs 1,100 sales assistants.
> 
> Sales assistants are paid the minimum wage. There is no training after an initial half-day induction, and no route to promotion except waiting for a supervisor to leave.
> 
> **Table 1.1: BF selected data**
> 
> | Shops | 62 |
> |---|---|
> | Sales assistants | 1,100 |
> | Annual labour turnover (%) | 68 |
> | Average length of service (months) | 7 |
> | Sales conversion rate, best shop (%) | 31 |
> | Sales conversion rate, worst shop (%) | 12 |
> 
> BF's new HR director has \$900,000 a year to spend on improving performance.

Analyse **two** ways BF could improve the performance of its sales assistants.
parts.solution_md:
One way is to provide proper training beyond the half-day induction **[K]**. BF's sales assistants currently receive nothing after their first morning, and conversion rates range from 12% in the worst shop to 31% in the best **[Ap]**. Teaching assistants how to approach customers, suggest additional items and handle hesitation would lift the weaker shops towards what the best already manage, and because conversion is a percentage of people already inside the shop, the gain costs BF nothing in extra footfall **[An]**. Moving the worst shops even halfway towards 31% would add substantial revenue from customers BF is already attracting **[An]** A second way is to create a route to promotion **[K]**. At present an assistant can only advance when a supervisor happens to leave, and BF loses 68% of its staff each year with average service of just seven months **[Ap]**. Someone who can see a path to a better-paid role has a reason both to stay and to perform well enough to earn it, whereas an assistant with no prospect of advancement has little reason to do more than the minimum **[An]**. Longer service also puts more experienced people on the shop floor, and experience is very likely what separates a 31% conversion rate from a 12% one **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Ashford (AF)**
> 
> Ashford (AF) assembles electronic control units for washing machines and ovens in country D. It employs 520 people and supplies four large appliance manufacturers.
> 
> AF's largest customer has warned that it will review the contract unless quality improves.
> 
> **Table 1.1: AF selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 520 |
> |---|---|
> | Units assembled per day | 9,400 |
> | Units failing final inspection (%) | 8 |
> | Units returned by customers after delivery (%) | 2.1 |
> | Cost of rework and replacement last year (\$000) | 780 |
> | Share of revenue from the largest customer (%) | 39 |
> 
> AF's production manager says the failures are concentrated among a group of assemblers who have not met the required standard for several months.

Analyse **two** consequences for AF of poor employee performance.
parts.solution_md:
One consequence is the cost of putting the work right **[K]**. Eight per cent of AF's 9,400 daily units fail final inspection, and rework and replacement cost \$780,000 last year **[Ap]**. Every unit reworked uses materials, machine time and labour AF has already paid for once, so the business is effectively producing part of its output twice while being paid for it once **[An]**. That \$780,000 comes straight out of profit, and it also occupies capacity AF could otherwise use to assemble units it could actually sell **[An]** A second consequence is that AF's most important customer relationship is now at risk **[K]**. That customer provides 39% of AF's revenue and has warned it will review the contract unless quality improves, with 2.1% of units already being returned after delivery **[Ap]**. A manufacturer of washing machines cannot tolerate control units that fail once fitted, because the cost of a fault reaching the end customer falls on them **[An]**. If AF loses that contract it loses nearly two fifths of its revenue at a stroke, a far larger loss than the rework bill, and one on which 520 employees depend **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Redwood (RW)**
> 
> Redwood (RW) is an accountancy practice in country H employing 240 accountants across five offices.
> 
> Accountants are currently told at the start of each year that they should "work hard and look after clients". Their pay rise is decided by a partner at the end of the year, and staff say they do not know what the rise is based on.
> 
> **Table 1.1: RW selected data**
> 
> | Accountants | 240 |
> |---|---|
> | Offices | 5 |
> | Accountants saying they understand how their performance is judged (%) | 24 |
> | Annual staff turnover (%) | 27 |
> | Fee income per accountant (\$000) | 96 |
> | Fee income per accountant in the highest-performing office (\$000) | 131 |
> 
> RW's senior partner has proposed introducing Management by Objectives, with each accountant agreeing three measurable objectives with a manager every six months.

Analyse **two** benefits to RW of introducing Management by Objectives.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that accountants would know exactly what is expected of them **[K]**. At present RW tells staff only to work hard and look after clients, and just 24% say they understand how their performance is judged **[Ap]**. Agreeing three measurable objectives every six months replaces that vagueness with something an accountant can actually aim at, so effort goes towards what RW values rather than towards whatever each person assumes matters **[An]**. That should help close the gap between average fee income of \$96,000 per accountant and the \$131,000 achieved in RW's best office **[An]** A second benefit is that pay decisions would become far easier to justify **[K]**. Rises are currently decided by a partner at the end of the year with no stated basis, and RW loses 27% of its accountants annually **[Ap]**. If a rise follows from objectives agreed in advance, an accountant can see why they received what they did, which removes the suspicion that rewards depend on which partner happens to know them best **[An]**. parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Fernbank (FB)**
> 
> Fernbank (FB) provides IT support to small businesses in country C. It employs 85 technicians who visit customers or resolve problems by telephone.
> 
> FB currently judges technician performance by the number of jobs each one closes per week.
> 
> **Table 1.1: FB selected data**
> 
> | Technicians | 85 |
> |---|---|
> | Average jobs closed per technician per week | 24 |
> | Jobs where the customer contacted FB again about the same problem within a week (%) | 19 |
> | Customer satisfaction score (out of 10) | 6.1 |
> 
> FB's operations manager thinks the current measure may be encouraging technicians to close jobs before problems are properly fixed.

Explain **one** other way FB could measure the performance of its technicians.
parts.solution_md:
One way would be to measure how many problems are solved at the first visit **[1]**. FB currently counts jobs closed per week, but 19% of jobs bring the customer back within a week about the same problem, so a closed job does not necessarily mean a solved one **[1]**. Counting only jobs that stay solved would reward technicians for fixing a fault properly rather than quickly, which should also lift a customer satisfaction score currently standing at 6.1 out of 10 **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Employee performance can be measured through output, quality, error or rework rates, customer feedback, absence, punctuality, or achievement of agreed objectives
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Measuring first-time fixes rather than jobs closed captures whether a problem was actually solved, addressing the 19% of jobs that recur within a week
> - Customer satisfaction ratings for individual technicians would show which staff customers are happiest with, which a count of jobs cannot reveal
> - Time taken per job could be combined with the repeat rate, so speed is judged alongside whether the work lasted
> - Any single measure can be gamed, so FB would do better to combine two or three rather than replace one narrow measure with another
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When suggesting a measure, say what it would show and be alert to what it would miss. Counting jobs closed rewards speed; counting first-time fixes rewards doing the job properly. Recognising that a measure changes behaviour, not just records it, is what lifts an answer to the top of the mark range.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** benefit to a business of using artificial intelligence in human resource management.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that AI can sort large numbers of job applications quickly **[1]**. A business advertising a popular vacancy may receive hundreds of applications, and AI can rank them against the requirements far faster than a person could read them **[1]**. This shortens the time between advertising and interviewing, which matters because strong candidates often accept another offer while a slower employer is still reading applications **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - AI can be used in HRM to screen applications, analyse patterns in absence or turnover, personalise training, schedule shifts, and answer routine employee queries
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Screening large volumes of applications quickly shortens the gap between advertising and interviewing, helping a business secure candidates before competitors do
> - Analysing absence and turnover data can reveal patterns a manager would not notice, such as one shift or department losing staff faster than others
> - Automated systems can answer routine questions about holiday entitlement or pay, freeing HR staff for work needing judgement
> - AI-based scheduling can match staffing to expected demand more precisely, reducing both overstaffing and gaps in cover
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Be careful not to overclaim for new technology. AI is good at handling volume and spotting patterns; it does not replace judgement, and screening tools can repeat bias present in past decisions. An answer showing awareness of what the technology actually does, rather than treating it as a solution to everything, reads as far more credible.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** way information technology is used in human resource management.
parts.solution_md:
One way IT is used in HRM is to manage recruitment **[1]**. Software can advertise a vacancy on several websites at once, collect applications in one place, and filter out candidates who do not meet the essential requirements **[1]**. This saves the HR department a great deal of time on early sorting, so staff can spend it interviewing the strongest applicants and the business fills the vacancy more quickly **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - IT is used in HRM for recruitment, record keeping, payroll, monitoring performance, delivering training, and planning future workforce needs
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Recruitment software advertises vacancies widely, gathers applications centrally and filters unsuitable candidates, saving HR staff time on early sorting
> - Digital personnel records let managers find information on qualifications, absence and training instantly rather than searching paper files
> - Online training modules can be completed at a time that suits each employee, so training does not require everyone to leave work at once
> - Workforce planning software can identify how many employees will retire in coming years, letting HR recruit and train replacements in advance
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Questions about technology in a business function reward naming the task, not the technology. Saying a business "uses computers" explains nothing; saying it uses software to filter job applications identifies the work being done. Start with the HR task, then say what the technology does to it.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Larkspur (LS)**
> 
> Larkspur (LS) operates 46 travel agency branches in country W, employing 390 consultants who sell holidays to walk-in customers.
> 
> Consultants are paid a fixed salary. Their performance is reviewed once a year in a meeting with a branch manager, and no targets are set between reviews.
> 
> **Table 1.1: LS selected data**
> 
> | Branches | 46 |
> |---|---|
> | Consultants | 390 |
> | Average sales per consultant per week (\$) | 4,100 |
> | Sales per consultant in the best-performing branch (\$) | 7,300 |
> | Consultants saying their annual review was useful (%) | 19 |
> 
> LS's HR director has proposed introducing quarterly objectives agreed between each consultant and their manager.

Explain **one** way LS's proposal could improve employee performance.
parts.solution_md:
One way is that quarterly objectives would give consultants something specific to work towards **[1]**. At present LS sets no targets between annual reviews, and only 19% of consultants find those reviews useful **[1]**. Agreeing objectives every three months means a consultant knows what is expected while there is still time to act on it, so someone selling well below the \$7,300 a week achieved in the best branch could be helped to improve during the year rather than being told about it twelve months later **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Performance can be improved through target setting, training, financial and non-financial incentives, better management, job redesign, or more frequent feedback
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Quarterly objectives replace a single annual conversation, so problems are identified while there is still time to address them
> - Only 19% of consultants find the annual review useful, so more frequent and specific discussion is likely to be taken more seriously
> - The gap between \$4,100 average weekly sales and \$7,300 in the best branch suggests substantial room to improve, and objectives make that gap visible to each consultant
> - Objectives agreed rather than imposed tend to gain more commitment, since a consultant who has helped set a target is more likely to accept it as fair
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A strategy earns marks when you show how it changes what people actually do. Setting objectives works because employees then know what to aim at and get feedback in time to act. Answers that name a strategy and assert it will "motivate staff" stop short of the mechanism, and usually stop short of the third mark too.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Eastvale (EV)**
> 
> Eastvale (EV) operates a warehouse in country S, packing and dispatching online orders. It employs 480 staff, of whom 310 are on temporary contracts.
> 
> Staff are set an individual target of 140 items packed per hour. A screen above each packing station shows how each worker is performing against that target.
> 
> **Table 1.1: EV selected data**
> 
> | Employees | 480 |
> |---|---|
> | Staff on temporary contracts | 310 |
> | Target items packed per hour | 140 |
> | Average items packed per hour | 112 |
> | Orders returned because of packing errors (%) | 6 |
> | Staff leaving within their first three months (%) | 41 |
> 
> Temporary staff receive one morning of training before starting work.

Explain **one** cause of poor employee performance at EV.
parts.solution_md:
One cause is that EV's staff receive very little training **[1]**. Temporary workers, who make up 310 of EV's 480 employees, are given only one morning of training before they begin packing **[1]**. Someone who has not been properly shown how to pack different items will be both slower and more likely to make mistakes, which helps explain why average output is 112 items an hour against a target of 140, and why 6% of orders come back because of packing errors **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Poor performance can be caused by inadequate training, unclear or unrealistic targets, weak motivation, poor working conditions, unsuitable equipment, or ineffective management
> 
> AO2
> 
> - One morning of training for temporary staff who make up nearly two thirds of the workforce leaves most employees learning the job while doing it
> - A target of 140 items an hour against an average of 112 may be unrealistic, and a target nobody reaches tends to discourage rather than motivate
> - Displaying each worker's performance on a screen above their station may raise pressure and errors rather than output, which fits the 6% return rate
> - With 41% of staff leaving within three months, EV constantly has inexperienced people packing, so average performance stays low however many are recruited
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Take care to name the cause rather than the symptom. Low output and packing errors are what poor performance looks like; the cause is what produced them, such as inadequate training. Examiners want the step behind the problem, so ask yourself why the figures are as they are before you start writing.

Flexi-time is an arrangement allowing employees to choose when they start and finish work **[1]**, provided they work an agreed total number of hours and are present during any core hours the business sets **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A working arrangement letting employees vary their start and finish times within limits set by the employer
> - A system where the total hours worked are fixed but the timing is partly chosen by the employee
> - An arrangement combining employee choice over hours with a requirement to be present at agreed core times

> **[exam-tip]**
> With arrangement terms, say what varies and what stays fixed. Under flexi-time the timing varies but the total hours do not. Answers stating only that employees "choose their hours" suggest they can also choose how many, which is a different arrangement altogether.

Labour productivity is a measure of output per worker over a period of time **[1]**, calculated by dividing total output by the number of employees **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Output per employee in a given period, found by dividing total output by the number of workers
> - A measure of how much each worker produces, used to compare performance over time or between businesses
> - The quantity of goods or services produced per unit of labour employed

> **[exam-tip]**
> Where a term is a ratio, say what is divided by what. Labour productivity is output divided by the number of workers. Giving the formula as well as the meaning is the surest way to earn both marks, and it takes only a few extra words.

Management by Objectives is a system in which managers and employees agree individual objectives that support the objectives of the business **[1]**, and performance is then reviewed against those agreed objectives **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A process in which each employee's targets are agreed with their manager and aligned with the organisation's overall objectives
> - A system of setting individual objectives derived from company objectives, with progress reviewed at regular intervals
> - An approach where employees are managed and appraised according to whether they achieve objectives agreed in advance

> **[exam-tip]**
> Named systems have a defining mechanism, and for MBO it is that objectives are agreed between manager and employee rather than simply imposed, then used to review performance. Naming who sets the objectives and what happens afterwards is what distinguishes MBO from ordinary target setting.

A zero hours contract is an employment contract that does not guarantee the employee any set number of hours **[1]**, so the business offers work only when it is needed and the employee is paid only for hours actually worked **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A contract under which an employer is not obliged to provide any minimum hours of work
> - An arrangement where hours vary according to demand and the employee is paid only for the hours worked
> - A flexible contract giving the business the right to call on an employee as required, without committing to regular hours

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a contract term, say what is guaranteed and what is not. Here nothing is guaranteed: no minimum hours, and pay only for hours actually worked. Definitions describing the contract as "flexible" capture the effect but not the substance, so state the absence of guaranteed hours explicitly.

Hard HRM is an approach that treats employees as a resource to be used as efficiently as possible **[1]**, hiring, deploying and releasing them according to what the business needs at the time **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An approach viewing employees as a cost to be controlled and a resource to be deployed wherever the business needs them
> - HRM focused on efficiency, with staffing levels adjusted to demand and decisions taken with little consultation
> - Managing people primarily to meet the organisation's needs, using short-term contracts and close control rather than long-term development

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word "hard" describes how employees are viewed, not how the manager behaves. A hard HRM approach treats staff as a resource to be used efficiently. Answers describing a manager who is strict or unkind miss the point, because the term is about the underlying view of labour, not about personality.

Urban Bee Hive (UBH) Co-working After Amit Menda graduated from university, he started work for a business in the US. The business specialised in designing workplace environments that aim to improve productivity. Whilst working in the US, Amit observed the growth of co-working. Co-working provides office space and support services for businesses. It offers a flexible solution for businesses which need an alternative to traditional long-term leasing or ownership of office space. In 2018, using his knowledge and experience, Amit founded UBH, a private limited company. It is based in country W, where co-working is still a relatively new idea. UBH focuses on providing office space to entrepreneurs and small businesses as and when they demand it. UBH calls its co-working centres ‘beehives’. There are three shareholders in UBH, all of whom are directors. Amit owns 50% of the shares while the other two shareholders own 25% each. A difficult economic climate Until 2020, UBH’s expansion was rapid. This internal growth was mainly financed by bank loans. However, in 2020 UBH came close to failing. There was a recession in country W when economic output fell by 10%. Many of UBH’s small business customers became insolvent during the recession. UBH was left with significant unused capacity and almost no working capital. The government responded quickly to the recession and made the following changes to its economic policies: • increased investment in infrastructure including road and rail transport • reduced income tax • reduced central bank interest rates • delayed payment of business and property taxes. Amit believes that without these changes to economic policies UBH would have failed. Marketing strategy UBH’s marketing strategy has targeted entrepreneurs starting new businesses and small, established businesses. Each UBH co-working centre (beehive) provides customers with shared kitchen facilities and snack vending machines. Customers are offered flexible contracts from 1 day to 1 year. The Marketing Director has produced a situational analysis for the Board of Directors to consider. Managing co-working centres and Human Resource Management (HRM) Amit has delegated authority to centre managers to make decisions about local advertising, day-to-day operational issues and hiring of employees such as cleaners, IT technicians and security. Each UBH beehive also has a customer relationship manager. UBH encourages its beehives to hold special events to promote their facilities and increase customer interaction. Recent events include educational talks and business advice sessions. UBH employees have flexible employment contracts. Employees can spend 5% of their time working on individual projects of interest. All new recruits receive extensive training. UBH’s vision includes ‘Our people are our greatest strength and we are committed to providing opportunities for each individual to fulfil their potential. Beehive 811 UBH is scheduled to open its new centre, Beehive 811, very soon.
